The orange lines radiating from Messier 77’s brilliant centre are not jets from its black hole. They are diffraction spikes, produced as light bends around the telescope’s structures.

That distinction changes how you read this James Webb Space Telescope portrait. The nucleus is bright enough to produce spikes across the image, but those lines are not arms or other structures belonging to M77. They are a pattern made by the telescope, not the galaxy.

Messier 77 is a barred spiral galaxy 45 million light-years away in Cetus. Its brilliant centre shines through swirling dust, bringing matter heating around a central black hole into the same view as stars forming throughout the dusty disc.

The blue has a different explanation. Webb’s Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) records the glow of interstellar dust grains, represented here in blue. Reading the portrait means separating that dust emission from the orange diffraction pattern around the nucleus.

In our latest cosmic-gallery post, we look at how black-hole activity and star formation share this galaxy. The image gives you both processes to consider, rather than only the brilliant centre that first catches your eye.

Read the light as well as the shapes: not everything radiating from a galaxy’s core belongs to the galaxy.

Here is the breakdown of why I believe this was either a fully staged event or a hijacked murder, and why I no longer trust a single thing the media or authorities have told us.

A 44-foot wingspan does not fit into a 30-foot crater without leaving massive structural shards protruding from the dirt. The power lines right next to the impact are still standing. I will admit, the ATC audio is soul-killing. It sounds like a real pilot trapped in a plane with dead controls. But no matter how heart-wrenching it is, I have to disregard it. Why? Because "Jack" is a ghost.

There is no Jack on the manifest. The name "Jack" was pulled directly from an April tweet made by the victim, Adam Robinson, months before the crash. The audio is AI-generated. The scriptwriters wanted a tragic, full-circle moment and inserted a keyword from the victim's social media into her dying words. 

They just didn't expect the internet to cross-reference the manifest and realize Jack doesn't exist. It was a sloppy script error.

I don’t know exactly what happened, but I know what didn't happen. There was no normal plane crash.

A) A Fully Staged Event: No one died. The crater was an explosive charge. The "tech bro" (Adam Robinson) and his family were extracted or disappeared. The media fed us AI images and fake audio to cover up a massive financial or political scandal.

Please don't go big on any of these unless you see reasons otherwise. These are all pretty much value-lean shots. I'm hoping to catch some bad lines, but I know these could all lose. This includes my Jets collaboration play. They are all going to be half a unit.

𝐑𝐄𝐃 𝐖𝐈𝐍𝐆𝐒 𝐌𝐋 +𝟐𝟑𝟑 (𝟎.𝟓𝐮)
I think there's an understanding that an underdog team like Detroit isn't necessarily expected to beat both Florida teams on back-to-back nights. That said, I really like what Todd McLellan has done with this Wings team this year. They're playing with a competitive edge, and watching yesterday's game, you could see how much fight this group has. Even when the Panthers were launching a full-on assault offensively, Detroit just kept pushing and never really backed down.

I also think the Detroit core is seriously underrated. DeBrincat, Raymond, Seider, and some of the younger guys like Finnie and MBN don't get nearly enough recognition, largely because this team still doesn't get much respect. The reality is that Detroit keeps finding ways to win games nobody expects them to, and I think tonight could be another one of those situations.

I'm also not too concerned about the back-to-back fatigue here. The travel wasn't particularly demanding, and I actually think the Wings could feed off yesterday's performance rather than come out looking exhausted or out of sync. They seem to have a bit of momentum behind them right now.

On the other side, the Kucherov situation can't be helping Tampa's locker room. Obviously, this is just speculation, but I wouldn't be surprised if some chemistry starts to erode the longer this situation drags on without a trade.

All things considered, I think Detroit is worth a serious look tonight.

𝐌𝐚𝐦𝐦𝐨𝐭𝐡/𝐌𝐚𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐟𝐬 𝐔𝐍𝐃𝐄𝐑 𝟕 (𝟎.𝟓𝐮)
This isn't a great value play, but some books have gone as high as 7, which I think is pretty high. At -130s to -140s, though, I don't think it's worth more than half a unit. Toronto just snapped a 5-game OVER streak, and I think things slow down for them a bit. Utah is coming off two high-scoring games, but giving up 6 goals to the Flyers should be enough to get them to tighten things up against a potent offense. Plus, I don't see either team wanting another run-and-gun game like their recent meeting.

𝐅𝐋𝐘𝐄𝐑𝐒 𝐌𝐋 +𝟏𝟔𝟐 (𝟎.𝟓𝐮)
Philly has been a bit unpredictable since bouncing back from that brutal 7-game start to the season, but I think the books are putting a little too much weight on those early struggles. Combine that with Minnesota being elite and looking like the contender everyone expected them to be, and I think we've ended up with a pretty lopsided line.

One thing that I don't think is getting nearly enough attention is the massive boost Philly just got with Cam York, Travis Konecny, and Owen Tippett returning. We already saw the impact in their last game. This team now has three lines with legitimate offensive firepower and looks much more complete defensively, which should only make things easier on a goaltending group that's already been overall fine.

Cates has also started to find his game after a slow start, Zegras and Michkov look like they're already in midseason form, and Martone is starting to come around as well. There's a lot to like here, and this is a team that should be capable of hanging with just about anyone.

Minnesota is absolutely legit, and when they're playing their best, they can beat anyone too. But that's kind of my point: I see these teams as much closer than the odds suggest. At +162, Philly feels like a coin-flip type of play to me.

𝐎𝐈𝐋𝐄𝐑𝐒 𝐌𝐋 +𝟏𝟑𝟖 (𝟎.𝟓𝐮)
Could this be a trap? Maybe, but I'm not fully buying it. I think two things are going on with this line:

1. Edmonton's injury impact is being way overblown.

2.NJ is a contender that's still riding the Hellebuyck hype, and they're playing at home.

Sure, it sucks that Hyman is out again, and the Oilers' goaltending concerns are valid. But I really think Babcock's system is overriding those factors. The game plan is pretty simple: everyone outside the big three just needs to make life easier for whoever's in net and take turns chipping in offensively. 

As long as the big three (McDavid, Draisaitl, and Bouchard) are in the lineup and everyone else sticks to their role, Edmonton can beat anyone, even with an AHL goalie in the Oilers net (they just did). There's a reason 8 of the Oilers' 13 games have seen their opponents score two goals or fewer. And if they need to get into a foot race and match the other team's offense, they can do that too. They've already beaten both the worst and the best team in the league in run-and-gun games.

The Devils are definitely not just any team, but I still think they're being heavily overpriced here, unless something happened in NYC over the past two days that we're not aware of.

𝐏𝐑𝐄𝐃𝐀𝐓𝐎𝐑𝐒 𝐌𝐋 +𝟏𝟕𝟐 (𝟎.𝟓𝐮)
Carolina has been nearly unstoppable and hasn't missed a beat since winning the Cup. But sometimes, it's a random-ass team that catches a powerhouse off guard in a mid-week game. Nashville is exactly that kind of team. Nobody really knows where they stand, which makes them a tough team to prepare for. They're also an unusually veteran-heavy group, with aging players making up the core, and that can go either way on any given night. However, those players are still highly impactful, and some are even playing some of the best hockey of their recent careers. Even the acquisition of Shane Wright fits that "unknown" theme. This is exactly the type of game where the Hurricanes could get caught sleeping, much like the Avs did when they rolled into Nashville and got absolutely blown out just over a week ago.

Songs and Goals
Put me in coach, I'm ready to play
(J.C. Fogerty brings some order to the world)
Sports and music are two parallel, almost overlapping fields. Let's examine the matter:
In both, there are eternal superstars (The Beatles and Bob Dylan, as well as Michael Jordan, Manchester United, and the New York Yankees), ordinary stars (Uriah Heep and Styx, for instance, versus Inter Milan, the Cleveland Browns, and the Atlanta Braves), and just plain divas (ummm... Def Leppard or the New York Jets...).
Fans stand at the very heart of both fields. Only a football fan's love for their team can be compared to a fan's devotion to Led Zeppelin (as depicted in the movie Almost Famous).
Fan wars – who said the Lakers versus the Celtics? Who whispered The Stones versus The Beatles? Did someone mumble Manchester United versus Liverpool? Did I hear Deep Purple versus Led Zeppelin? The Eagles versus Fleetwood Mac? Could it be Barcelona versus Real Madrid? Is it possible that Jennifer Lopez vs. Beyoncé?!
There are no other fields that funnel so much cultural and social interest – through extensive press coverage, films about the genre, etc. In the eyes of fans, in both cases, it's nothing short of a religion. So how is it that these fields are parallel and almost never meet? This seems like a paradox. Well, that's not quite accurate. Here are ten songs that, despite everything, caused a slight stir in the world of sports, or are identified with a specific profession, sporting event, team, etc. Ten small stories about people. Enjoy.
________________________________________
CENTERFIELD – John Fogerty (Baseball)
John Fogerty, former leader of the band CCR, ended the hardest decade of his life in 1985. It was the decade after his debut album marked his transition to a solo career and his final break from CCR, under whose leadership he achieved worldwide fame as one of America's most important songwriters. The past decade had made people forget (even Americans, who sanctify their cultural ethos) just how much Fogerty himself was Mr. Rock 'n' Roll. His continuous silence was broken only by sporadic public outbursts of anger and rage at the other band members who "stole" his glory, legal battles with greedy producers, and other nonsense. But in 1985, America was happy to embrace its favorite son again (and indeed its FORTUNATE SON). Fogerty, for his part, returned with a brave embrace, releasing an album full of old-school, rootsy rock 'n' roll, as only he can deliver. At the heart of the album was the title track (bearing the same name...), dealing with the ultimate American leisure experience – a baseball game. The song has long become such a symbol of American sports that every fan knows how to hum it. A re-reading of the lyrics: "Put me in, Coach - I'm ready to play today; Look at me, I can be Centerfield," reveals that no less than John Fogerty aimed at what was happening on the playing field – he was also aiming at the audience and the music industry, and at his return to center stage.
________________________________________
Gerry And the Pacemakers - You'll Never Walk Alone (Football)
"You'll Never Walk Alone, Liverpool." This is what fans of the English team, for many years dubbed "the best team in the world" (and not just by their fans), sing every Sunday (even if it's on a Saturday!). The undisputed anthem was inherited by the fans of Kenny Dalglish, Ian Rush, Graeme Souness, Michael Owen, and other greats who starred on the Anfield pitch – from a band called Gerry and the Pacemakers, originally from... Liverpool, of course! (It's actually Gerry and the Pacemakers' rendition of a famous song by Rodgers and Hammerstein – two of Broadway's greatest writers). Liverpool is the ultimate meeting point between sport and music; it seems there is no other place in the world, besides Manchester of course (and also New York – but more on that another time), where local residents are convinced of the supremacy of their music idols (The Beatles) and their football heroes. The place that gave birth to the FAB FOUR of the whole world – The Beatles – also brought forth a paler version of them - Gerry and The Pacemakers. Music critics often note the connection between Gerry's group and Paul and John's, who operated in the same place and at the same time, played in a similar style (but not with identical quality, of course), participated in the British Invasion, dominated the pop charts, and even shared a music producer – Brian Epstein. Rock history has shown who survived the 60s in the hearts of fans. But for Liverpool fans, none of those matters; Gerry and the guys' version of the song has become their anthem. And remember, as you walk through a storm – hold your heads up high – and don't be afraid of the dark – you'll never walk alone.
________________________________________
WONDERWALL – OASIS (Football)
"You'll Never Walk Alone, Liverpool – Manchester will always walk beside you (and try to overtake you) ..." I doubt (in fact, we are all convinced it wasn't the case) if, when Dickens wrote his book "A Tale of Two Cities," he foresaw the colossal city war between Liverpool and Manchester. Billions of words have already been poured out about the sporting rivalry between these two leading cities in the birthplace of football, truly. But it seems that in the field of music, unlike on the green pitch, the Manchester lads struggled more to stand against The Beatles and their city. Nevertheless – Manchester found some musical righteous ones to push them, if not to equality, then at least to a close game. Starting with Herman's Hermits in the 60s and their sugary mega-hits, moving through the Madchester craze (also called Madchester, what a silly pun) of the late 80s, which began with the immortal STONE ROSES, continued with Happy Mondays, and finally reached its peak in the mid-90s with the Gallagher brothers, the leaders of OASIS. What does all this have to do with sports? Oh, right – the Manchester Blues (City) fans bother to sing before and during every game their best songs, which are primarily corrupted lyrics of well-known songs for the glorification of their idols. One of the most preferred of these songs is "Wonderwall." Here you go.
________________________________________
Na Na Hey Hey (Kiss Him Goodbye) - STEAM (Basketball mostly, but everything really)
What is the most classic story in sports? And what is the most classic story in music? You guessed right these are the stories of Cinderella and the one-hit wonder. For a fan of a football team languishing at the bottom of League G Central, there's no greater dream than an unforgettable performance and a victory in the cup final against the mighty champion, against all odds. For every guitar strummer in a slum in the suburbs of a small town in the middle of nowhere – there's no greater dream than hitting one song that will break through to the top of the charts. STEAM is an excellent example of this story – a band that came out of nowhere – launched one eternal hit in late 1969 and disappeared into the melancholic sunset, leaving no other mark on the world. It's unclear how or why exactly – but to this day, the hysterical rhythm of the catchiest chorus ever ("Na Na Na Na, Na Na Na Na, Hey Hey Hey, Goodbye") has been played thousands of times in every stadium around the globe that respects itself. So, we are left to wonder whether the thousands of spectators at the arena are cheering for the team or paying tribute to STEAM and all Cinderella stories ever told...
________________________________________
We Will Rock You - WE ARE THE CHAMPIONS - Queen (anything with or without a ball)
Ah, we've reached Freddie Mercury's gang, my heart's delight (those who recognize irony – recognize it correctly). It's impossible to escape this song (in fact, the two opening tracks of the News of the World album played consecutively). It's so identified with sports events that the listener is forced to accept it as an integral part of the event, as a kind of reminder to all of us that Queen will not disappear from our lives, no matter how hard we try to suppress those disgusting years.
What's the secret of the song? Well, unlike the case of STEAM, here the answer is clear. The band (QUEEN) was and still is one of the most recognized and beloved rock bands of all time. The song itself gives the average sports viewer everything he's looking for – an opportunity to warm up and get into the rhythm with clapping, followed by a cheesy ballad with Brian May's drawn-out guitar riffs (bordering on a new genre I call neo-kitsch-fascist) praising the collective as undisputed champions. Freddie and the band's memorable performances at the holy temple of football (Wembley Stadium) – certainly contributed to the fact that to this day, it is forbidden to enter any final match before memorizing the lyrics of the aforementioned song.
________________________________________
Eye Of the Tiger – Survivor (Boxing)
How much money can one make from the success of a single hit? How many years can a career be stretched out based on one brilliant idea? The band Survivor and Sylvester Stallone (Rocky to you) prove that the answers are – a lot and a very, very lot... The story of Rocky is the great American dream story: a boy born into the wrong conditions (a poor Italian family, a brain smaller than a pea, and verbal expression skills suitable for a developmentally challenged child in a tough day-care), a child grows into a boy and a man who fails in all his endeavours, the child discovers that everyone has something they're good at (exploding and disfiguring other faces until they're as ugly as his own, in this specific case), a failing man gets a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for worldwide fame against the world champion, a man wins the fight (it took him two movies, damn it), a man falls in love with a woman, millions of children go to the cinema and watch this story for 5 dollars. A film wins an Oscar; a man becomes a millionaire. End of story.
End of story? No, not really. Like Sylvester Stallone, the band "Survivor" also refused to disappear into the horizon after releasing one of the most killer hits of all time for the soundtrack of Rocky 3 (also known as Rocky vs. Mr. T). Instead, they insisted on sticking around to write more mini hits for Rocky 4 and other such trivialities. Their main fame today they owe to appearances on American talk shows, in a recurring skit that is full of amusing humor about them repeatedly reminiscing about the "good old days" when they achieved fame. What they don't realize is that the joke is on them...
________________________________________
Hurricane - Bob Dylan (Boxing)
Bob Dylan opens his wonderful album, DESIRE (1975), with one of his most recognized pieces. The song tells the life story of Rubin Carter, who was a heavyweight boxing champion stripped of his title after being convicted of murder. Dylan became convinced, after visiting him in prison and speaking with Carter, that the Black boxer was framed and innocent. Dylan publishes his defense in the best way known to the free world – he writes a song. The melody is simple – three or four chords that any child can play with guitar accompaniment in a fast, monotonous rhythm and a lot of Dylan's nasal singing (the "reading" of the text lasts over 8 minutes...) with a background of drums and percussion. It's so simple that even Mashina adopted the rhythm and melody for a song of their own (Geveret Sara Hashchena) – regrettably, they completely forgot about the boxer Rubin Carter.
________________________________________
Zevon, Warren - Werewolves of London (Billiards)
A few clarifications – Snooker is not a sport in my eyes (even if it's called billiards) – in sports, you sweat, and not because you're embarrassing yourself in front of friends! Nevertheless, I found it appropriate to include it in the framework of this column – just so such an important artist as Warren Zevon would receive some light that he so deserves (and so lacks). However, this song easily enters all my "sporty" lists for an entirely different reason – the motif named after OZZY, none other than the COMEBACK! Is there anything better than a sporting or musical comeback story?! What am I talking about? So, in 1986, Martin Scorsese's film "The Color of Money" was released, starring Paul Newman and Tom Cruise. Scorsese asked his good friend (not for the first time or last) Robbie Robertson, formerly the leader of THE BAND, to produce and edit the soundtrack for the film. The two had already been good friends since Scorsese's days as a fan of the band and as the director of the film documenting their farewell performance – THE LAST WALTZ. Since then, they had already collaborated on Scorsese's spectacular film – Raging Bull (1980, starring Robert De Niro). For this film (The Color of Money), Robertson chose mostly blues-infused pieces, but among them, he placed our friend, Warren Zevon, with this catchy song, complete with the bar-like piano atmosphere so characteristic of him (everyone remembers the arrogant Cruise "dancing" with his cue, while defeating his opponents on the POOL table). The song itself had already been a hit seven years prior to the film's release, and its reappearance on the big screen (a mini comeback) re-established Warren Zevon's fame as one of the sharpest American writers. So, where's the real comeback? Here it comes. The film earned Paul Newman recognition for his abilities once again (after a long time), and more importantly, his sole Oscar win. Since then, it's customary to say that Newman received this award essentially for lifetime achievement, because the Academy members were simply tired of the fact that one of America's favorite sons was "drying up" and aging without an Oscar.
________________________________________
Mrs. Robinson – Simon & Garfunkel (Baseball, roughly)
"Mrs. Robinson" is not a song about sports, it's not played at sports events, it's not performed by athletes (unless you call the juggling manipulations Paul Simon has been performing with his hair for years – sport) and it belongs to a film soundtrack (The Graduate) that has no connection to sports whatsoever. So, what, for God's sake, is it doing here?! It's thanks to one eternal line (one of the most justified lines...) that mentions baseball legend Joe DiMaggio (who was also Marilyn Monroe's partner for a short period): "Where have you gone, Joe DiMaggio Our nation turns its lonely eyes to you" – a line that has long become a line of longing and nostalgia for a simpler, clearer America of the past. And what's more American than Joe DiMaggio?! The film, written during a time of social turmoil and upheaval in the US, is a symbol of those times. This line is America's declaration during that period.
________________________________________
Sa Le'at (Drive Slowly) – Arik Einstein (Eating the fans' hearts. A kind of sport that only exists in the Holy Land)
"And I think Hapoel lost again, and how pitiful the fans are – they're eating their hearts out. Drive slowly, drive slowly." Arik Einstein (he's one of us. Correction – he's us) is the most famous die-hard sports fan in Israel, and himself an excellent former athlete (Israeli high jump champion). This is without mentioning his being the nation's greatest when it comes to founding and renewing Hebrew rock. But it's all nonsense – Einstein, a true genius worthy of the name, was always a little more interested in the Hapoel Tel Aviv football team than in music. And this is an example of the impossible dissonance at the heart of every sports lover, who dedicates his life and soul to worshipping a cheap imitation of sport, instead of turning to things with real substance. But it's not done by choice – as they've said before: three things you don't choose in life – your father, your mother, and your football team...
